sections.h2: How fast can you sell a house in Austin?
sections.html:
Speed in Austin depends on the route you pick and on how clean the paperwork is. A cash buyer can close in a matter of weeks, while a listing runs on the buyer's lender and inspection calendar. Austin is the seat of Mower County in southeast Minnesota, so most of the paperwork runs through the Mower County offices on First Street NE.

You have three basic routes:

  • Sell on the open market and wait for financing and appraisal.
  • Sell privately to a neighbor, relative or investor and handle the paperwork yourself.
  • Accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house with every repair left to them.

Before any buyer walks through, you can shorten the timeline by sorting out four things: the permit history of the house, the property tax status, any city charges tied to the parcel, and whether the lot sits in an area that flooded in the past. The sections below cover each one.

Austin has 26,689 residents, and buyers are mostly local workers, first-time purchasers and investors. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $163,900, far below the figures in the Twin Cities suburbs. These are the numbers a seller is most likely to compare against an offer.

Austin housing figures, 2020 to 2024

Typical home value (owner-occupied)$163,900

The same-house rate is 87.0 percent, so the market turns over slowly and a well-priced home stands out. At $953 a month, median rent is low as well, which is why some Austin owners keep a house as a rental and others decide to sell it. If you are weighing that choice, read the rental registration rules below first.

Many Austin homes were built in the Cedar River floodplain, and buyers and lenders ask about it. The city's flood history lists major floods in July 1978, 1983, 1993, spring 2000 when the Cedar River crested at 23.4 feet, September 2004 and 2010. Dobbins Creek and Turtle Creek also run through town.

The city answered with buyouts. Flood-prone homes were purchased and demolished using a Community Development Block Grant and the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program, low areas were turned into parks, dikes were added after 2004, and a flood wall protecting downtown was finished in 2014. If your lot is near the river or one of the creeks, ask City Hall at 500 4th Avenue NE for the parcel's floodplain status before you list, and ask your insurance agent what flood coverage costs.

Tornadoes are the other weather risk on record. An EF2 tornado crossed the northwest and north side of Austin on June 17, 2009. Roof age, siding and tree condition are the details a buyer's inspector will notice.

Check your permit record first. The city warns that if you sell a building with modifications done without a permit, you may be required to tear the addition down, leave it unoccupied or pay for costly repairs. Permits are usually needed for additions, decks, garages, fences, pools, water heaters, re-roofing and electrical, plumbing and heating work.

Two routine ordinances also generate liens against sellers who ignore them.

  • Grass and weeds. City Code 10.13 sets an 8 inch height limit. After a notice from the weed inspector you have seven days to comply, then the city cuts it and certifies the cost to the Mower County Auditor as a special assessment collected like real estate taxes.
  • Sidewalk snow. Chapter 7.04 requires owners to clear public sidewalks within 12 hours after snow stops, and the city may clear them after 24 hours and bill the owner.

Deal with both before closing. Austin also does not allow chickens, which matters if you kept hens and a buyer asks about the coop.

If the house is a rental, Austin requires it to be registered under City Ordinance 4.29, and a Change of Ownership form must be filed when a rental is sold. Ask the city whether the same tenants will stay with the new owner, because that decides which form is used.

If you live elsewhere for part of the year, the program also asks you to name a local rental manager who handles emergencies and inspections. Anyone planning to keep the tenants will want to see the rental registration and any inspection results, so pull those documents together before a deal is signed.

sections.h2: Mower County property taxes at closing
sections.html:
Mower County bills property tax in two halves, due May 15 and October 15, and second-half agricultural tax is due November 15. The Auditor-Treasurer's office is in the Government Center at 201 First Street NE, Suite 7, in Austin, and the phone is 507-437-9535.

  • The county does not mail second-half statements, so a buyer should ask for the amount.
  • Mail payments are judged by postmark, and a private postage meter mark does not count.
  • The county will not accept post-dated checks.
  • A missing statement does not excuse a late payment.

On the deed side, Minnesota Statute 287.21 sets the state deed tax at .0033 of the net consideration when the price is above $3,000. An eCRV is required for sales over $3,000, and a deed cannot pass title while taxes are delinquent. A well statement or well disclosure certificate also has to accompany a transfer deed. Call the Mower County recorder for the local filing steps and fees.

sections.h2: What you must tell a buyer in writing
sections.html:
Minnesota Statute 513.55 requires a written disclosure of material facts you know before the purchase agreement is signed. It covers facts that could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment of the property, made in good faith and to the best of your knowledge. A separate radon statute, section 144.496, adds a written radon disclosure and a copy of the Minnesota Department of Health booklet.

For an Austin house, the facts buyers care about most are basement water, past flooding, roof and furnace age, and any work done without a permit. Writing these down early keeps negotiations short, and it matters even more in a quick sale where the buyer is not hiring an inspector.

A practical order of work: finish the disclosure, gather permits and any rental registration, get the tax amount from the Auditor-Treasurer, and clear any weed or snow charges. With those four done, a cash offer or a listing can move at its own pace without surprises at the table.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection from the city before selling in Austin?
faqs.a: Ask the building department at City Hall, 500 4th Avenue NE, whether any sale-time step applies to your address. Gather your permits and any rental registration so a buyer can see them.

faqs.q: What happens if I have unpermitted work on my Austin house?
faqs.a: You may be required to remove it, leave it unoccupied or pay for repairs. Ask the building office whether the work can be permitted after the fact before you list.

faqs.q: What are the due dates for Mower County tax?
faqs.a: May 15 and October 15, with second-half agricultural tax due November 15. The county does not mail second-half statements, so request the figure from the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-437-9535 if you need it for closing.

faqs.q: Can a high weed or grass notice block my sale?
faqs.a: Not by itself, but unpaid mowing costs become a special assessment on the parcel. Austin allows 8 inches of grass and gives seven days after notice, so cut it early and ask the clerk for any pending charges.

faqs.q: Is Austin a good place to sell to a landlord or investor?
faqs.a: Often yes. Median rent is $953 and 71.5 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so investors look at the town. A sold rental needs a Change of Ownership form filed with the city.
